title: The global economy is approaching a tipping point – and investors need to pay attention
gist: Wood Mackenzie upgraded its 2026 global GDP growth forecast to 2.5% on strategic reserve drawdowns, rerouted Gulf exports and an AI investment boom, but Peter Martin argues this resilience hinges entirely on the Strait of Hormuz reopening soon — with the AI race itself now driving stark regional divergence, from a 61%-of-GDP-growth AI dependency in the US to Europe falling behind on regulation, hyperscaler absence and grid limits.

themes.theme: Global growth resilience despite the US-Iran war

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie upgraded its baseline 2026 global GDP growth forecast to 2.5% (from 2.3%), with a recovery to 3.0% in 2027, even as the US-Iran war continues.
insights.speaker: Peter Martin
insights.so_what: An upward growth revision during an active regional war is a contrarian data point — it suggests markets pricing in war-driven recession risk may be behind the actual macro data, at least in the baseline scenario.
insights.quote: We now project global GDP growth of 2.5% in 2026, revised up from 2.3%, with a recovery to 3.0% in 2027.
insights.locator: How resilient is the global economy to the US-Iran conflict?

insights.claim: Three forces are doing the heavy lifting behind the upgraded growth forecast: strategic energy reserve drawdowns by major economies, the rerouting of Gulf energy exports, and a powerful AI investment boom injecting momentum into US and Asian growth.
insights.speaker: Peter Martin
insights.so_what: Two of the three growth drivers (reserve drawdowns, rerouted exports) are finite buffers being drawn down, not renewable sources of resilience — investors should ask how much runway remains in strategic reserves before this support fades.
insights.locator: Three forces are doing the heavy lifting

insights.claim: The entire resilience thesis rests on a single critical assumption — that normal energy transit through the Strait of Hormuz resumes soon — and if it does not, Peter Martin says the calculus changes entirely.
insights.speaker: Peter Martin
insights.so_what: This single point of failure means the baseline 2.5% growth forecast is fragile, not robust — investors should treat Hormuz transit status as the single most important macro indicator to monitor right now.
insights.quote: that resilience rests on a single critical assumption: that normal energy transit through the Strait of Hormuz resumes soon
insights.locator: How resilient is the global economy to the US-Iran conflict?

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's Extended Disruption scenario describes a credible (not tail-risk) path to global recession, involving exhausted strategic reserves, rationing, price spikes, soaring inflation, central bank tightening, and a contraction in developed economies.
insights.speaker: Peter Martin
insights.so_what: This scenario is explicitly framed as credible rather than tail risk — portfolio stress tests should model it as a real branch of outcomes, not an extreme edge case, particularly for inflation-sensitive and rate-sensitive positions.
insights.quote: Our Extended Disruption scenario is not a tail risk to be dismissed. It describes a credible path to global recession
insights.locator: What happens if Strait of Hormuz disruption persists?

insights.claim: The collapse of the US-Iran memorandum of understanding in June has already delayed Wood Mackenzie's baseline resolution timeline for the conflict.
insights.speaker: Peter Martin
insights.so_what: A concrete diplomatic failure (the June MoU collapse) has already pushed out the resolution timeline once — a precedent that should lower confidence in any near-term resolution date currently being priced by markets.
insights.quote: The collapse of the US-Iran MoU in June has already delayed our baseline resolution timeline.
insights.locator: What happens if Strait of Hormuz disruption persists?

insights.claim: Peter Martin argues the tipping point in the global economy is real and closer than many market participants appear to be pricing in.
insights.speaker: Peter Martin
insights.so_what: An explicit claim that the market is underpricing tail risk is itself a tradeable view — worth weighing against current credit spreads and volatility pricing for Middle East-exposed and energy-sensitive assets.
insights.quote: The tipping point is real, and it is closer than many market participants appear to be pricing in.
insights.locator: What happens if Strait of Hormuz disruption persists?

themes.theme: Middle East: contraction now, diversification as buffer

insights.claim: Iraq, Kuwait, Iran and Qatar are all forecast to contract in 2026, and Saudi Arabia's GDP contracted 4.8% year-on-year in Q2 2026, though its decade of economic diversification — non-oil revenue now at 46% of government income, up from 27% in 2015 — gives it meaningfully more shock-absorption capacity than a decade ago.
insights.speaker: Peter Martin
insights.so_what: Saudi Arabia's diversification (46% non-oil government revenue vs 27% in 2015) is a measurable buffer that differentiates it from other Gulf states now contracting — a reason to expect Saudi assets to outperform regional peers through this shock.
insights.quote: non-oil revenues now at 46% of government income, up from 27% in 2015
insights.locator: Middle East: Iraq, Kuwait, Iran and Qatar are forecast to contract

insights.claim: A sharp Middle East regional rebound of 7.5% GDP growth is forecast for 2027 as oil production recovers.
insights.speaker: Peter Martin
insights.so_what: The 2026 contraction-to-2027 rebound pattern implies Middle East risk assets could be a V-shaped recovery trade once oil production normalizes, rewarding investors willing to hold through 2026 volatility.
insights.quote: A sharp regional rebound of 7.5% GDP growth in 2027 is forecast as oil production recovers.
insights.locator: Middle East: Iraq, Kuwait, Iran and Qatar are forecast to contract

themes.theme: Asia's AI supply chain boom and concentration risk

insights.claim: Taiwan, South Korea and Malaysia are the standout winners of the AI supply chain boom, with their combined exports surging more than 40% year-on-year in H1 2026.
insights.speaker: Peter Martin
insights.so_what: A greater-than-40% YoY export surge across three economies is a strong, measurable proxy for AI hardware demand — useful as a leading indicator for semiconductor and AI-hardware supply chain revenue trends.
insights.quote: combined exports surging more than 40% year-on-year in H1
insights.locator: Asia: Taiwan, South Korea and Malaysia are the standout winners

insights.claim: Taiwan's Q1 GDP growth of 14.5% year-on-year signals both the scale of opportunity and the concentration risk building in AI-linked manufacturing.
insights.speaker: Peter Martin
insights.so_what: Wood Mackenzie itself flags concentration risk alongside the growth story — a 14.5% GDP print driven by one sector is a warning sign for economic diversification, not just a bullish headline, for anyone modeling Taiwan risk.
insights.quote: Taiwan’s Q1 GDP growth of 14.5% year-on-year signals the scale of opportunity (and concentration risk) in AI-linked manufacturing.
insights.locator: Asia: Taiwan, South Korea and Malaysia are the standout winners

themes.theme: US growth is an AI capex story

insights.claim: The AI investment wave accounted for an estimated 61% of US GDP growth in H1 2026, making it the US economy's primary growth engine.
insights.speaker: Peter Martin
insights.so_what: With AI capex responsible for the majority of US growth, any deceleration in hyperscaler capital spending would have an outsized, immediate effect on headline US GDP — a key macro risk to monitor via quarterly capex guidance.
insights.quote: The AI investment wave – we estimate it accounted for 61% of US GDP growth in H1 2026 - is the economy’s primary growth engine.
insights.locator: United States: The AI investment wave

insights.claim: Top-five tech company capex is set to exceed $700 billion in 2026, even as the Federal Reserve holds rates restrictive at 3.75%.
insights.speaker: Peter Martin
insights.so_what: Over $700 billion in tech capex proceeding despite restrictive 3.75% rates shows AI investment is largely rate-insensitive right now — a data point for debating whether monetary tightening can meaningfully cool the AI capex cycle.
insights.quote: With top-five tech capex set to exceed US$700 billion in 2026, the structural tailwind is significant, even as monetary policy remains restrictive with rates held at 3.75%.
insights.locator: United States: The AI investment wave

insights.claim: The US economy's heavy reliance on AI capex for growth, combined with a restrictive 3.75% policy rate, leaves little monetary-policy room to offset a slowdown if AI investment decelerates.
insights.speaker: Peter Martin
insights.so_what: This is an implied structural vulnerability: a single-sector growth engine paired with limited rate-cut headroom means an AI capex slowdown could hit US GDP with less policy cushion than in a typical cycle.
insights.locator: United States: The AI investment wave

themes.theme: Europe falling behind in the AI race

insights.claim: EU-27 GDP growth is forecast at just 1.1% in 2026, well behind the US and Asia, as Europe fails to capture the high-margin value of AI intellectual property due to regulatory constraints, a lack of domestic hyperscalers, and grid limitations on data centre buildout.
insights.speaker: Peter Martin
insights.so_what: Europe's growth gap is attributed to specific, addressable structural causes (regulation, hyperscaler absence, grid capacity) rather than cyclical weakness — useful for assessing whether EU policy interventions could actually close the gap versus a permanent structural disadvantage.
insights.quote: Europe is failing to capture the high-margin value of AI intellectual property, hampered by regulatory constraints, a lack of domestic hyperscalers, and grid limitations on data centre buildout.
insights.locator: Europe: The region is falling behind

insights.claim: The US government's June decision to block foreign access to advanced AI models adds a further strategic complication to Europe's ability to catch up in the AI race.
insights.speaker: Peter Martin
insights.so_what: US export-control style restrictions on advanced AI model access widen the US-Europe AI capability gap further, reinforcing the case that Europe's underperformance versus the US is now also policy-driven from outside its own borders.
insights.quote: The US government’s June decision to block foreign access to advanced AI models adds a further strategic complication.
insights.locator: Europe: The region is falling behind

insights.claim: The US-China AI race, supply chain rewiring and energy security pressures are structural, not temporary, forces that will fragment global trade into two distinct blocs and reshape commodity demand, infrastructure investment and credit conditions for years to come.
insights.speaker: Peter Martin
insights.so_what: Treating bloc fragmentation as structural rather than cyclical means investors should build two-bloc supply chain and trade-flow assumptions into long-horizon models, not wait for a return to pre-fragmentation trade patterns.
insights.quote: the era of elevated geopolitical risk is not temporary. The US-China AI race, supply chain rewiring, and energy security pressures are structural forces that will fragment global trade into two distinct blocs
insights.locator: How is geopolitical fragmentation reshaping the global economy?

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's long-term model projects global real GDP rising from US$99 trillion in 2025 to US$213 trillion by 2060, though demographic headwinds and geopolitical fragmentation represent genuine downside risks to that trajectory.
insights.speaker: Peter Martin
insights.so_what: A more-than-doubling of global GDP by 2060 is the long-run bull case, but Wood Mackenzie itself flags demographics and fragmentation as genuine (not token) downside risks — worth weighting when using this figure as a long-horizon planning anchor.
insights.quote: global real GDP rising from US$99 trillion in 2025 to US$213 trillion by 2060
insights.locator: closing paragraph before the report download call-to-action
